items.text: In this lesson you meet new people. You say hello and spell your name. You ask: What's your name?
Two people meet at work. They say hello. They say: My name is Tomasz. They ask: What's your name? Then they say: Nice to meet you. At the end, they say goodbye.

Say your name in two ways. I am Mei. My name is Mei. I and am go together. My name and is go together. To ask, say: What is your name? Say please when you ask for something. Say thank you when you get it.
Next, you read a class list. Find the names on it. Write your name on the list. Use capital letters: MEI. Then copy your name two times.
Then you meet a new classmate. Say hello and your name. Spell your name: A-N-A. Then ask: What's your name?
Last, you read a short story. People meet and say hello. Read it two times.
You meet a new person. What do you say?
Hello, Samir. Nice to meet you.
Are you Mei? Yes, I am.
Is your name May? No, it is Mei.
Write your name on the list.
Copy your name from your card.
My English class is in Room 4.
Nice to meet you. How do you spell Tomasz?

I am, my name is. I am + your name: I am Mei. My name is + your name: My name is Mei. Ask: What is your name? Short: What's your name? Yes, I am. No, I am not. A coffee, please. Thank you. Sorry, I am late.
items.speech: I am, my name is. I am + your name: I am Mei. My name is + your name: My name is Mei. Ask: What is your name? Short: What's your name? Yes, I am. No, I am not. A coffee, please. Thank you. Sorry, I am late.

In this lesson you count to twenty. You say your age and phone number. You ask: How much is it?
Numbers are everywhere. Carlos joins a sports centre. The receptionist asks: How old are you? She asks for his phone number. Carlos asks: How much is it? Listen for fifteen and fifty.

Count with me: one, two, three … twenty. Eleven and twelve are new words. Thirteen to nineteen end in teen. Thirty-four is thirty and four. Say phone numbers figure by figure. Stop after three or four figures.
Next, you read a price list. Read the prices slowly. Then you write 0 to 20. And you write numbers about you.
Then you swap numbers with a friend. Write the number down. Say it back to check it. Ask two prices. How much is the tea?
Last, you read a short story. It has numbers in it. Read it two times. Find the numbers.
Where do you use numbers every day?
How many people are here today?
Write your age on the form.
My phone number starts with zero.
What's the price of the milk?
My money is in my bag.

Numbers and phone numbers. 11 eleven · 12 twelve · 13 to 19 end in -teen. 20 twenty · 30 thirty · 40 forty · 50 fifty How many + things? How many classes? Three. Phone numbers: figure by figure, in small groups. 0 is zero or oh. 4 4 is double four.

In this lesson you talk about people. You say: This is my sister. You show a family photo.
Samir is at a work party. His family is there too. His friend Lena asks: Who is that? Samir says: That's my son. He's six. Listen for he and she. Listen for this and that too.
A man or a boy: he. A woman or a girl: she. This is near you. That is far away. Before a person: my, your, his, her. My sister. His wife. Her son.
Next, you read a text: My family. Then you fill in a family form. Write names and numbers.
Then you show a family photo. Say who everyone is. This is my mother. Then say one more thing. Her name is Rosa.
Last, you read a family story. Who is in the family? Read it two times.
I call my family every Sunday.
My father is in the photo.
My brother works in a hotel.
Their new baby is a girl.
Omar is my friend from work.
This is a photo of my family.
Hi, Lena. This is my wife, Leila.
That's my son, Adam. He's six.
Her name is Nadia. She's nine.

he and she · this and that · my, his, her. A man or a boy: he. A woman or a girl: she. Near you: this. Far away: that. This is my sister. That's my brother. I → my · you → your · he → his · she → her His name is Adam. Her name is Nadia.
items.speech: he and she · this and that · my, his, her. A man or a boy: he. A woman or a girl: she. Near you: this. Far away: that. This is my sister. That's my brother. I → my · you → your · he → his · she → her. His name is Adam. Her name is Nadia.

In this lesson, you name everyday things. You say their colour and size. You ask for things at work.
It is Mei's first day at work. She needs some things. She asks Tomasz for a pen. Can I have a pen, please? Tomasz asks: Which one? Mei says: The blue one, please.
Say a or an before one thing. A pen. A key. An umbrella. Say an before a, e, i, o and u. The colour comes first. A red bag. Not: a bag red. Ask: What colour is it? It's red.
Next, you read about Amina's bag. Then you read a notice. It says what to bring to work. Then you write a list of things.
Then you ask for six things. Say the colour or the size. Say: The small one, please. The other person finds the right one.
Last, you read a short story. Read it once for the story. Then read it again. Answer the questions.
You start a new job. What do you need?
Can I have a pen, please?
I read a book on the bus.
This is the key for the office.
Can I have the red umbrella?
The small key is for the office.
My mobile is in my bag.
Can I have a pencil, please?
I have a bottle of water.
Can I have an umbrella, please?
Write a list of six things.
A black pen and a book.
Hi, Tomasz. Can I have a pen, please?
Thank you. And what is this?
OK. Can I have an umbrella, please?
a and an, and colours. a + thing: a pen, a key. an + a, e, i, o, u: an umbrella. Colour or size first: a red bag. Ask: What colour is it? It's blue. Which one? The black one, please.
items.speech: a and an, and colours. a + thing: a pen, a key. an + a, e, i, o, u: an umbrella. Colour or size first: a red bag. Ask: What colour is it? It's blue. Which one? The black one, please.

This lesson is about your home. You say where you live. You say where things are.
Samir and Mei work together. Samir asks Mei: Where do you live? Mei says: I live in a flat. She says what is in it. Listen for the rooms. A kitchen, a bedroom, a bathroom.

Small words say where. In, on, under, next to. The keys are on the table. Say there is for one thing. There is a kitchen. Say there are for two or more. There are two chairs. My is for you. Our is for you and other people.
Next, you read about Kwame's flat. Then you read a building notice. Then you write where your things are.
Then you talk about your home. A friend listens and draws it. Say the rooms and where they are. Is the picture right?
My bed is under the window.
They live in a big house.
I live in a small flat.
The bathroom is next to the bedroom.
The keys are on the table.
The chair is next to the table.
My bedroom has a big window.
The stairs are next to the lift.
I live in a flat. It's new!
No, it's small. There are three rooms.
Yes. My bed is under the window.
And you? Where do you live?

Where things are. Where is the bed? It's under the window. in, on, under, next to: It's on the table. There is + one: There is a kitchen. There are + two or more: There are two chairs. my = me. our = me and other people.
items.speech: Where things are. Where is the bed? It's under the window. in, on, under, next to: It's on the table. There is + one: There is a kitchen. There are + two or more: There are two chairs. my = me. our = me and other people.

This lesson is about food and drink. You say what you like. You order in a café.
Carlos is in a café near work. He orders tea. I'd like a cup of tea, please. The worker asks: Anything else? Carlos is hungry. He wants a sandwich. Then he asks: How much is it?
Like is about always. I like tea. I don't like coffee. Want is about now. I'm thirsty. I want water now. In a café, say I'd like. I'd like a tea, please. Say: I'm hungry. Not: I have hungry.
Next, you read a café price list. Then Omar says what he eats. Then you write a shopping list.
Then you order in a café. Ask for a drink and some food. Ask: How much is it? Then pay.
You are in a café. What do you drink?
I'd like a cup of tea, please.
I drink juice in the morning.
Can I have a cup of coffee?
I'm hungry. Can I have a sandwich?
Egg, please. I don't like fish.
Like, want, and I'm hungry. Always: I like tea. I don't like coffee. Now: I'm thirsty. I want water. Café: I'd like a tea, please. I'm hungry. I'm thirsty. Not: I have hungry.
items.speech: Like, want, and I'm hungry. Always: I like tea. I don't like coffee. Now: I'm thirsty. I want water. Café: I'd like a tea, please. I'm hungry. I'm thirsty. Not: I have hungry.

This lesson is about clothes and weather. You buy a coat in a shop. You say what you are wearing.
This lesson is about clothes and weather. First, Mei is in a shop. She wants a coat. Listen for the weather. It's cold, and it's raining. Mei asks: Can I try it on? Then she says: It's too big.

For the weather, start with it. It's hot. It's cold. It's raining. For your clothes now, say: I'm wearing. I'm wearing a hat. Too big is a problem. Too small is a problem too. Put on means start wearing. Take off means stop wearing.
Next, you read about Tomasz. It's a cold morning. He puts on his clothes for work. At work, there is a notice. It says what to wear. Then you write about your clothes today.
Then you need clothes for tomorrow. It's cold, with rain. You go to a shop. The jumper is too big. Say: Can I have a smaller size, please?
Last, you read a short story. It's about clothes and weather. Read it once for the story. Then read it again.
It's cold outside. What do you put on?
Let's eat outside in the sun.
The wind is very cold today.
Put on your coat. It's cold.
I wear a white shirt at work.
Can I try these shoes on?
It's cold. Put on a jumper.
Put on your coat. It's raining.
It's hot. Take off your hat.
Yes, please. I want a coat.
It's very cold, and it's raining.
Thank you. Can I try it on?

The weather and your clothes. The weather: It is hot. It is cold. It is raining. Clothes now: I am wearing a coat. She is wearing a hat. A problem: It is too big. It is too small. Put on means start wearing. Take off means stop wearing. Ask: What's the weather like?
items.speech: The weather and your clothes. The weather: It is hot. It is cold. It is raining. Clothes now: I am wearing a coat. She is wearing a hat. A problem: It is too big. It is too small. Put on means start wearing. Take off means stop wearing. Ask: What's the weather like?

This lesson is about your body. You say where it hurts. You ask for help.
This lesson is about your health. First, Kwame is ill. He is with the doctor. The doctor asks: Where does it hurt? Kwame says: My head hurts. And my back. Then he asks: Can you help me?
Where does it hurt? Say my, a body part, and hurts. My head hurts. My back hurts. For two feet, say: My feet hurt. For how you feel, say I am. I am ill. I am tired. Do not say: I have tired.
Next, you read a sign. It is for ill people. It says: Ill? Tell the desk your name. Then you write a note. It is for the doctor. Say how you feel. Say where it hurts.
Then you are at work. You feel ill. Tell someone. Say where it hurts. Then ask: Can you call a doctor, please?
Last, you read a short story. It is about health. Read it once for the story. Then read it again.
You feel ill at work. What do you do first?
My arm hurts. I can't work.
My hand hurts. I can't write.
My leg hurts. I can't walk.
My foot hurts in these shoes.
My tooth hurts. I can't eat.
I'm ill today. I can't go to work.
I want to see a doctor.
The hospital is near my home.
Can you call a doctor, please?
Put your hand on your heart.
My head hurts. And my back.
Two days. Can you help me?

How you feel, and where it hurts. My + part of the body + hurts: My head hurts. My back hurts. Two feet, two eyes: My feet hurt. My eyes hurt. I am + how you feel: I am ill. I am tired. Ask for help: Can you help me, please? The doctor asks: Where does it hurt?

This lesson is about places in town. You ask the way. You say the answer back to check.
This lesson is about places in town. First, Amina asks the way. She says: Excuse me. Where is the bank, please? A man says: Go straight on. Then go left. He speaks fast. Amina says: Slowly, please.
Start with excuse me. Then ask: Where is the bank, please? Listen for left, right and straight on. Then say it back, to check. Straight on, then left? Your voice goes up at the end.
Next, you read signs in town. A sign says open or closed. A sign says exit. Arrows show the way. Then write the way to your home.
Then ask the way to three places. Say each answer back. Left? Next to the bank? Is it fast? Say: Slowly, please.
Last, you read a short story. It is about a town. Read it once for the story. Then read it again.
You are new in a town. What do you do?
Excuse me. Where is the bank, please?
Excuse me. Where is the station?
I work in a small shop.
I buy fruit at the market.
The bus stop is on the right.
The bank is on the left.
Go straight on to the station.
Can you say it slowly, please?
Is it far? No, it isn't.
Read the sign on the door.
The bank is closed on Sunday.
My flat is on Mill Road.
Is this the way to the station?
On the right. Is it far?
Next to the market? Thank you.

Asking the way. Ask: Excuse me. Where is the bank, please? The way: Go left. Go right. Go straight on. Where it is: It's on the left. It's on the right. Say it back to check: Straight on, then left? Too fast? Say: Slowly, please.

This lesson is about work. You say your job and times. You say what you do every day.
This lesson is about your work. First, two people meet. They are Lena and Samir. Lena asks: What do you do? Samir says: I'm a cleaner. I work at the hospital. Then she asks: What time do you start?
Say a before your job. I'm a cleaner. Not: I'm cleaner. Say at before a time. I start at eight. In the morning. In the afternoon. In the evening. But: at night. And days: on Monday, on Sunday.
Next, read a notice at a café. It has work hours and days off. It has opening times too. Then write about your day and week.
A new person comes to your work. Say your job and your hours. Say your day off. Then ask: And you?
Last, you read a short story. It is about work. Read it once for the story. Then read it again.
When do you like to work?
I start at ten at night.
I work at a big hotel.
I'm a cleaner at the hospital.
I'm a student. I'm learning English.

I finish at four in the afternoon.
I'm at home in the evening.
I work five days a week.
Hello. I'm Samir. Nice to meet you.
I'm a cleaner. I work at the hospital.
Yes. I finish at six in the morning. And you?

Jobs and times. A job: I am a teacher. He is a driver. A time: I start at eight. I finish at four. in the morning, in the afternoon, in the evening at night, on Monday, on Sunday Ask: What do you do? What time do you start?
